questions.q: In an IAM policy statement, what does the Resource field control?
options: Which IAM user is allowed to sign in from a given IP range
Which specific resource ARNs (or ARN patterns) the statement's Action and Effect apply to
How long the temporary credentials issued by the statement remain valid
Which AWS region the policy document itself is stored in
questions.explain: Resource lists the ARNs (or ARN patterns) a statement applies to. Scoping it tightly — instead of using "*" — limits the blast radius of an otherwise-correct Action grant.

questions.q: Why is "Resource": "*" risky even when Action is scoped to only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket?
options: It grants read access to every bucket in the account instead of just the one the policy was meant for
It has no real effect because Resource is ignored when Action is already scoped
It forces MFA on every request automatically
It is syntactically invalid and IAM will reject the policy at creation time
questions.explain: Resource and Action apply independently. A tightly scoped Action combined with a wildcard Resource still lets the principal act on every matching resource in the account, including ones created later.

questions.q: In IAM's policy evaluation logic, what happens when one applicable policy has an explicit Deny and another has an explicit Allow for the same request?
options: The Allow and Deny cancel out, so the request is evaluated as if neither policy existed
Whichever policy was attached most recently takes precedence
The Allow wins if it comes from an AWS-managed policy
The request is denied — an explicit Deny anywhere in the evaluation always overrides any matching Allow
questions.explain: IAM evaluation logic gives explicit Deny statements absolute precedence: if any applicable policy explicitly denies the action, the request is denied regardless of how many policies allow it.

questions.q: What does the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition key do when added to an Allow statement?
options: It restricts the grant to only apply when the calling principal authenticated with MFA in the current session
It automatically enables MFA on the IAM user the policy is attached to
It is a resource-based policy field, not a condition key, and cannot be used in identity-based policies
It blocks the action entirely regardless of the Effect field
questions.explain: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is a condition key that narrows a grant so it only takes effect when the request was made under an MFA-authenticated session — a common way to gate destructive actions.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between an AWS-managed policy and a customer-managed policy?
options: Customer-managed policies cannot include a Condition field
AWS-managed policies only ever use Deny statements
An AWS-managed policy is fixed and cannot be edited, while a customer-managed policy is your own versioned document you can tailor and reuse
There is no real difference — both are evaluated by a different engine
questions.explain: AWS-managed policies (like AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess) are convenient but fixed and often broader than one job needs. Customer-managed policies are your own, editable, versioned JSON documents attached to the principals that need them.
